title: Most of Whittier, Alaska Lives in One Building. Why?
question: Why do people live in Whittier?
message: This video tells curious adults that almost a whole Alaskan town lives in one building because the US Army built a hidden, ice-free wartime port there and left its barracks behind, and in that weather one building is the sensible choice.
angle: People live in Whittier because the US Army picked this foggy, ice-free inlet for a hidden wartime port, drilled a tunnel to reach it and left behind a fourteen-storey building that became the town, despite a one-lane tunnel that locks at night and around twenty feet of snow a year.

scenes.narration: I reached the only road into town one minute after it closed. The road was a tunnel. The tunnel had gone to bed. I was holding the timetable. I had not read it. Hi, I'm Wob. I visit odd places and ask why anyone stays.

scenes.narration: So I slept in the car, with the roof down, because I had not figured out the roof yet. On the other side of that mountain is Whittier, Alaska, a small port on a long grey inlet. Most of the people who live there share one front door. One building, fourteen floors. I came here to move in. By morning I had questions. Why build a town behind a mountain that closes at night? And why would almost everyone end up in the same building? Before this trip was over, I had both answers, and I changed my mind about living here more than once.

scenes.narration: In the morning I joined the queue at the staging area and finally read the timetable. In winter, the tunnel opens at seven in the morning, and the gate locks at eleven at night. Cars and trains take turns, in fifteen-minute windows, one direction at a time. Picture a one-lane bridge with a traffic light. Now make the bridge about two and a half miles long, roughly four kilometres, and let a train borrow it. A train borrowed it. My window slid past while I counted carriages. Then the next window opened, for traffic coming the other way. I waved at them. They did not wave back. They were busy reading their timetables. The timetable says unscheduled trains can hold things up by fifteen to thirty minutes. It also had a note about cars like mine.

scenes.narration: My rental was a convertible. Convertibles have to close their roofs before going in, so I wrestled mine up while the whole queue watched. Then there is the cold rule. When it is thirty-two Fahrenheit or below, that's zero Celsius, traffic only goes in during the last five minutes of each window. Finally the light turned green. Inside, the road and the railway share the same strip of concrete, with the rails sunk right into the lane. It is the longest combined rail and highway tunnel in North America, and cars have only been allowed through since two thousand. I kept both hands on the wheel and did not breathe until daylight. Rock on both sides. Rails under my tyres. Somewhere behind me, my courage.

scenes.narration: Out the far side, the clouds sat so low I could have worn one. Grey water. Waterfalls. Mountains going straight up out of the sea. So why put a town here? My guess was gold. I was not completely wrong about people passing through. For thousands of years the Chugach, an Alutiiq people, crossed Portage Pass behind this inlet to trade with Dena'ina people on Cook Inlet. In the late eighteen hundreds, gold seekers hauled sleds over the same pass. But hauling sleds is not the same as building a tower. Gold did not build this town. Weather did.

scenes.narration: Turns out the fog was a selling point. During the Second World War, the US Army wanted a supply port in Alaska, and this inlet had a lot going for it. The water is deep and does not freeze, so ships could come in all year. According to the state's tunnel history, going on to Seward added about fifty-two miles of sailing. And the low cloud and fog helped hide the port from Japanese planes. From the air, the fog was a blanket pulled over the harbour. To connect the port to the rest of Alaska, the Army built a railway through two mountains, finished on April the twenty-third, nineteen forty-three. The longer tunnel is named after Anton Anderson, the Army engineer in charge. By the mid nineteen forties, more than a thousand soldiers and civilians lived here. I put my sunglasses away. I also forgave the tunnel. It was never built for my car.

scenes.narration: Back home, I unfold the timetable on my desk, because this is the point where my trip went indoors. After the war, the Army put up two huge buildings in Whittier. One of them is why my mail had a floor number. The Hodge Building, now called Begich Towers, is fourteen floors of pale concrete, finished in nineteen fifty-seven after going up in three sections. According to local news, nearly everyone in town lives inside it. The twenty twenty census counted about two hundred and seventy people, and estimates vary a little since then.

scenes.narration: So I spent one winter day without going outside. Morning: I went down for my mail in my slippers. The post office is inside the building, close to the entrance. So is the police station. Late morning: the clinic, then the convenience store for snacks. Afternoon: laundry, still indoors, with my basket riding the elevator. There is a church in here too, plus city offices and a playground. Think of an apartment block where the whole town has moved into the lobby. And the school? It sits across the road, and children get there through a tunnel underneath. My boots never left the closet. They seemed relieved.

scenes.narration: From the lobby window I could see the other building. Nobody lives in it. The Buckner Building was finished in the early nineteen fifties, according to old Army records, with six floors for about a thousand soldiers. Inside were a movie theatre, a bowling alley and a small clinic. Before my tower, this was the town under one roof, and it did not stay full for long. The Army began pulling out around nineteen sixty, and records differ on when the last soldiers left. Today Buckner is a ruin. The windows are gone, there is asbestos inside, and the city fenced it off. So I looked at it from outside the fence, which is the only sensible way to see it. I imagined the bowling alley anyway.

scenes.narration: Then I made the mistake of stepping outside. One snowflake landed on my nose. Then its family arrived. Then the neighbours. By March, the snow on the ground here averages about forty-seven inches, roughly one point two metres. I am shorter than that. Over a whole year, Whittier gets somewhere around twenty feet of snow, about six metres, and the official tables don't quite agree on the exact figure. Count the rain as well and you get roughly five metres of water a year, about sixteen feet. If none of it drained away, it would stand about as tall as a two-storey house.

scenes.role: chương 4 (tiếp): gió, sóng, không quá lạnh mà ướt; Wob đổi ý lần 1 (chuyển tới nhưng không ra ngoài)
scenes.narration: The wind joined in. It averages ten to fifteen miles an hour. But the state's tunnel weather page says it often blows forty to sixty, with waves of four to six feet out in the inlet. It rolled me back to the front door, gently, like a bouncer. Here's what surprised me. It isn't that cold. According to the weather records, January highs hover right around freezing. My first trip was colder than this by a lot. The problem is that everything is wet, all the time. My raincoat needed a raincoat. Back inside, dripping on the hallway floor, I changed my plan. I had come to move here and take long walks. New plan: move here and never go outside. Suddenly, a town in one building did not look odd. It looked like the sensible answer.

scenes.narration: I want to tell this part plainly. On March the twenty-seventh, nineteen sixty-four, a great earthquake struck southern Alaska. In Whittier, the quake and the waves that followed killed thirteen people. At the time, only about seventy people lived here. The waterfront was badly damaged. Today the port still works, and the town still stands where it stood. I stayed at the water for a while and did not try to be clever.

scenes.narration: I went back in July. Same tunnel. Different personality. In summer it opens at five thirty in the morning and stays open until eleven fifteen at night. I arrived one minute before closing, on purpose, and drove straight through. On the far side, the snow was gone and the mountains had turned green. Cruise ships tie up here now. Boats head out into Prince William Sound to see glaciers. People go fishing for halibut and salmon, or paddle kayaks along the shore. The quiet winter town had turned into a front door for the whole sound. The building was still there, of course, at the foot of the mountain. But now people were actually outside it, on purpose, in T-shirts. I put my slippers away and found my boots. They looked nervous.

y_hinh.y: Cắt cứng: cùng cổng hầm, cùng góc máy, giờ là mùa hè xanh; đồng hồ trên cổng '23:14'. Wob đội mũ lưỡi trai, không áo mưa, xe mui trần mở mui

scenes.role: chương 6 (tiếp): đường mòn Portage Pass, danh hiệu WWII Heritage City 10/2026; Wob đổi ý lần 2
scenes.narration: On my last day I hiked the Portage Pass trail, about two miles out toward Portage Lake, along the old route over the mountains. I wore my raincoat, just in case. It did not rain. I felt cheated. Back in town, I learned about a new title. In October twenty twenty-six, the National Park Service named Whittier an American World War Two Heritage City. Only one city per state gets it. The town is proud of the port that made it. And standing in the sun, I changed my mind again. Not forever. Just for the summer.

scenes.role: outro ở cổng hầm (không ở bàn): ghép các mảnh trên mặt sau tờ lịch, con dấu SUMMER ONLY, câu hỏi bình luận
scenes.narration: The back of the timetable was blank, so I drew the whole story on it. A war needed a port that ships could reach all year and planes could not see. The fog hid it. A tunnel reached it. The Army left, and its building became the town. And the weather makes living under one roof sensible instead of strange. So, do I move in? Summer only. From May to September, the tunnel runs until a quarter past eleven, and Whittier is a doorway to glaciers, fish and trails. In winter it means roughly twenty feet of snow, wind that rolls me into doors, and a road with a bedtime. Bring a calendar. Bring patience. Leave the habit of running late somewhere else. I taped the timetable to my dashboard. This time I read it. Could you spend a whole winter without stepping out of your building?

claims.quote: I reached the only road into town one minute after it closed
claims.statement: The only road access into Whittier, Alaska, is through the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel, which closes overnight.

claims.quote: Whittier, Alaska, a small port on a long grey inlet
claims.statement: Whittier, Alaska, is a port town on Passage Canal, an inlet of Prince William Sound.

claims.quote: Most of the people who live there share one front door
claims.statement: Most residents of Whittier, Alaska, live in a single building, Begich Towers.

claims.quote: One building, fourteen floors
claims.statement: Begich Towers in Whittier, Alaska, is a fourteen-storey building.

claims.quote: Why build a town behind a mountain that closes at night
claims.statement: The tunnel into Whittier, Alaska, closes to traffic at night.

claims.quote: In winter, the tunnel opens at seven in the morning, and the gate locks at eleven at night
claims.statement: In winter (October 1 to April 30), the Whittier tunnel operates from 7:00 a.m. to 10:45 p.m., and the gate is locked at 11:00 p.m.

claims.quote: Cars and trains take turns, in fifteen-minute windows, one direction at a time
claims.statement: The Whittier tunnel is a single lane shared by cars and trains, with traffic running one direction at a time in alternating fifteen-minute windows.

claims.quote: Now make the bridge about two and a half miles long, roughly four kilometres
claims.statement: The Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel through Maynard Mountain is about 2.5 miles (about 4 km) long.

claims.quote: unscheduled trains can hold things up by fifteen to thirty minutes
claims.statement: According to the Alaska DOT&PF tunnel schedule, unscheduled trains can delay tunnel traffic by fifteen to thirty minutes.

claims.quote: Convertibles have to close their roofs before going in
claims.statement: Convertibles must have their tops closed to travel through the Whittier tunnel.

claims.quote: When it is thirty-two Fahrenheit or below, that's zero Celsius, traffic only goes in during the last five minutes of each window
claims.statement: When temperatures are at or below 32°F (0°C), the Whittier tunnel opens only for the last five minutes of each scheduled opening window.

claims.quote: the road and the railway share the same strip of concrete, with the rails sunk right into the lane
claims.statement: In the Whittier tunnel, road vehicles and trains use the same single lane, with the railway set into the roadway.

claims.quote: It is the longest combined rail and highway tunnel in North America
claims.statement: The Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel is described as the longest combined rail and highway tunnel in North America.

claims.quote: cars have only been allowed through since two thousand
claims.statement: The Whittier tunnel opened to road vehicles in 2000.

claims.quote: For thousands of years the Chugach, an Alutiiq people, crossed Portage Pass behind this inlet to trade with Dena'ina people on Cook Inlet
claims.statement: For thousands of years, Chugach (Alutiiq) people used the Whittier area and crossed Portage Pass to trade with Dena'ina Athabascan people on Cook Inlet.

claims.quote: In the late eighteen hundreds, gold seekers hauled sleds over the same pass
claims.statement: In the late nineteenth century, gold prospectors hauled sleds over Portage Pass near Whittier.

claims.quote: During the Second World War, the US Army wanted a supply port in Alaska
claims.statement: During World War II, the US Army chose the Whittier inlet as a military supply port in Alaska.

claims.quote: The water is deep and does not freeze, so ships could come in all year
claims.statement: Whittier has a deep-water, ice-free port that can receive ships year-round.

claims.quote: going on to Seward added about fifty-two miles of sailing
claims.statement: According to Alaska DOT&PF's tunnel history, shipping on to Seward instead of Whittier added about 52 miles by sea.

claims.quote: the low cloud and fog helped hide the port from Japanese planes
claims.statement: Whittier's low clouds and fog helped conceal the port from Japanese aircraft during World War II, and its poor weather reduced the risk of bombing.

claims.quote: the Army built a railway through two mountains, finished on April the twenty-third, nineteen forty-three
claims.statement: The US Army's railway spur to Whittier, including tunnels through Begich Peak and Maynard Mountain, was completed on April 23, 1943.

claims.quote: The longer tunnel is named after Anton Anderson, the Army engineer in charge
claims.statement: The longer Whittier tunnel is named after Anton Anderson, the Army engineer who led its construction.

claims.quote: By the mid nineteen forties, more than a thousand soldiers and civilians lived here
claims.statement: By the mid-1940s, Whittier's population of soldiers and civilians exceeded 1,000.

claims.quote: After the war, the Army put up two huge buildings in Whittier
claims.statement: After World War II, the US Army built two large buildings in Whittier: the Buckner Building and the Hodge Building.

claims.quote: The Hodge Building, now called Begich Towers, is fourteen floors of pale concrete, finished in nineteen fifty-seven after going up in three sections
claims.statement: The Hodge Building in Whittier, now Begich Towers, is a fourteen-storey concrete building built in three sections between 1953 and 1957.

claims.quote: According to local news, nearly everyone in town lives inside it
claims.statement: Nearly all residents of Whittier, Alaska, live in Begich Towers; sources range from 'most' to 'every resident'.

claims.quote: The twenty twenty census counted about two hundred and seventy people, and estimates vary a little since then
claims.statement: The 2020 US Census counted about 270 people in Whittier, Alaska (sources give 272 or 278); later estimates are around 250.

claims.quote: The post office is inside the building, close to the entrance. So is the police station
claims.statement: Begich Towers in Whittier contains the post office, near the entrance, and the police station.

claims.quote: the clinic, then the convenience store
claims.statement: Begich Towers contains a health clinic and a convenience store.

claims.quote: There is a church in here too, plus city offices and a playground
claims.statement: Begich Towers also contains a church, city offices, a laundry and a playground.

claims.quote: It sits across the road, and children get there through a tunnel underneath
claims.statement: Whittier's school is across the road from Begich Towers and is reached by an underground tunnel.

claims.quote: The Buckner Building was finished in the early nineteen fifties, according to old Army records, with six floors for about a thousand soldiers. Inside were a movie theatre, a bowling alley and a small clinic.
claims.statement: The Buckner Building in Whittier was completed in the early 1950s (sources give 1953 or 1954), has six floors and was built for about 1,000 soldiers, with a theatre, a bowling alley and a small clinic (dispensary).

claims.quote: The Army began pulling out around nineteen sixty, and records differ on when the last soldiers left
claims.statement: The US Army began withdrawing from Whittier around 1960; sources differ on when the military fully left (some say 1960, others 1966).

claims.quote: Today Buckner is a ruin. The windows are gone, there is asbestos inside, and the city fenced it off. So I looked at it from outside the fence, which is the only sensible way to see it
claims.statement: The abandoned Buckner Building in Whittier has missing windows and asbestos inside, and the city has fenced it off.

claims.quote: By March, the snow on the ground here averages about forty-seven inches, roughly one point two metres
claims.statement: Average snow depth in Whittier in March is about 47 inches (about 1.2 m), based on 1942–2011 data.

claims.quote: Whittier gets somewhere around twenty feet of snow, about six metres, and the official tables don't quite agree on the exact figure
claims.statement: Whittier receives roughly 20 feet (about 6 m) of snow per year; the same Alaska DOT&PF page gives both 241 and 257 inches.

claims.quote: you get roughly five metres of water a year, about sixteen feet
claims.statement: Whittier's average annual precipitation is about 196 inches, roughly 5 metres (about 16 feet).

claims.quote: If none of it drained away, it would stand about as tall as a two-storey house
claims.statement: About 5 metres of water is roughly the height of a two-storey house (channel's own comparison based on Whittier's annual precipitation).

claims.quote: It averages ten to fifteen miles an hour. But the state's tunnel weather page says it often blows forty to sixty, with waves of four to six feet out in the inlet
claims.statement: According to Alaska DOT&PF, wind at Whittier averages 10–15 mph but often reaches 40–60 mph, with 4–6 foot waves in the middle of Passage Canal.

claims.quote: January highs hover right around freezing
claims.statement: Average January high temperatures in Whittier, Alaska, are around freezing: about 31°F in DOT&PF data (1942–2011) and about 33°F in NOAA 1991–2020 normals.

claims.quote: On March the twenty-seventh, nineteen sixty-four, a great earthquake struck southern Alaska
claims.statement: A great earthquake struck southern Alaska (Prince William Sound) on March 27, 1964.

claims.quote: In Whittier, the quake and the waves that followed killed thirteen people
claims.statement: The 1964 earthquake and the waves it generated killed 13 people in Whittier.

claims.quote: At the time, only about seventy people lived here
claims.statement: About 70 people lived in Whittier at the time of the 1964 earthquake.

claims.quote: The waterfront was badly damaged. Today the port still works
claims.statement: Whittier's waterfront was heavily damaged in 1964, and the port is still in operation today.

claims.quote: In summer it opens at five thirty in the morning and stays open until eleven fifteen at night
claims.statement: In summer (May 1 to September 30), the Whittier tunnel operates from 5:30 a.m. to 11:15 p.m.

claims.quote: Cruise ships tie up here now. Boats head out into Prince William Sound to see glaciers
claims.statement: Cruise ships call at Whittier, and glacier tours leave from Whittier into Prince William Sound.

claims.quote: People go fishing for halibut and salmon, or paddle kayaks along the shore
claims.statement: Halibut and salmon fishing and sea kayaking are popular visitor activities in Whittier.

claims.quote: I hiked the Portage Pass trail, about two miles out toward Portage Lake, along the old route over the mountains
claims.statement: The Portage Pass trail from Whittier runs about two miles toward Portage Lake, over a historic route across the mountains.

claims.quote: In October twenty twenty-six, the National Park Service named Whittier an American World War Two Heritage City. Only one city per state gets it
claims.statement: In October 2026, the National Park Service designated Whittier, Alaska, an American World War II Heritage City; the designation goes to one city per state.

claims.quote: In winter it means roughly twenty feet of snow
claims.statement: Whittier receives roughly 20 feet of snow per year (sources give 241 or 257 inches).

claims.quote: From May to September, the tunnel runs until a quarter past eleven
claims.statement: From May through September the Whittier tunnel runs its summer schedule until 11:15 p.m., and Whittier is a base for glacier tours, fishing and hiking.
